problem: Flyto2 Core is an execution kernel for automation and AI-agent workflows. Prior to 2.26.8, the earlier CVE-2026-67429 remediation applied validate_path_with_env_config() to only a hand-picked set of file-writing modules, leaving data.csv.write in src/core/modules/atomic/data/csv_write.py, data.json_to_csv in src/core/modules/atomic/data/json_to_csv.py, file.copy in src/core/modules/atomic/file/copy.py, and file.move in src/core/modules/atomic/file/move.py outside the FLYTO_SANDBOX_DIR confinement boundary. The advisory also identifies unguarded modules across the broader data.*, file.*, and report-writer families. data.csv.write relies on a.. substring denylist that does not reject absolute paths, while the other named modules accept caller-controlled output or destination paths without the canonical guard. A caller able to execute modules or recipes can therefore write attacker-controlled content outside the configured sandbox, potentially overwriting application code, recipes, startup files, scheduled-task files, or authorization files and gaining code execution on the host. This issue is fixed in version 2.26.8. Exploitable remotely over the network.
solution: Fixed in version 2.26.8 — update immediately. Canonicalize paths and restrict to an allowlisted directory. Update to the patched version.

problem: Flowintel disabled TLS certificate verification for all MISP API connections and used unverified SSL contexts for IMAP and SMTP STARTTLS mail connections. problem: Etherpad is a real-time collaborative editor. problem: In `github.com/eclipse-keypont/crypto11/v2` versions `<= 2.0.0-rc8` (and the deprecated v1 module paths `github.com/eclipse-keypont/crypto11 <= 1.6.8`, `github.com/ThalesGroup/crypto11 <= 1.7.0-rc1` and `github.com/ThalesIgnite/crypto11 <= 1.2.5`), the `cipher.AEAD` returned by `SecretKey.NewGCM()` passes whatever nonce it is given straight to `CK_GCM_PARAMS` without checking its length against `NonceSize()`, and accepts an empty nonce. On a token that accepts a zero-length GCM IV — SoftHSM2 does — every `Seal` with an empty nonce encrypts under the same IV, reusing the keystream and exposing the GHASH authentication key, which allows forgeries. Separately, `Config.UseGCMIVFromHSM` sends a NULL IV with length zero to the token unless `GCMIVFromHSMControl.SupplyIvForHSMGCMEncrypt` is also set, so the token has nowhere to write the IV it generates: a `Seal` with a non-empty nonce panics after the plaintext has already been encrypted, and a `Seal` with an empty nonce returns ciphertext under an empty IV without error. On the v1 line HSM-IV mode additionally never copies the token-generated IV back to the caller, so the caller keeps its own nonce while the data was encrypted under another one. Exploitable remotely over the network.

problem: pretix offloads certain processes to background tasks that are run by a different server to avoid HTTP workers being clogged with processes that take longer than a usual web request. The browser periodically polls the server to see if the task is already finished using a UUID-shaped task ID. Once the task is completed, pretix resumes to the next step of the operation based on the result of the task. The system does however not check if the result stems from the correct type of task. Therefore, an attacker can supply the UUID of a task of a different type and pretix will continue with the result from the wrong task. In most cases, this will just result in an error because the return types do not match up, but in some cases this can be abused to extract objects the attacker usually should not see. Specifically, a vector was discovered that allowed to abuse this for unauthorized access to other people's ticket purchases. The attacker can, however, not control which purchases they get access to. Exploitable remotely over the network.

The donation receipt processes an attacker-controlled first name through the V3 template engine and then reprocesses the result through the legacy `{meta_donor_*}` engine, which can disclose the donor's email-access bearer token. The donor-dashboard password endpoint accepts that token by itself and calls `wp_set_password()` for the WordPress user linked to the donor. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to reset the password of any WordPress account linked to a GiveWP donor record and gain access to that account. If the linked account is an administrator, the attacker can achieve full site compromise and remote code execution through standard administrator functionality. A published GiveWP form with a usable gateway, enabled donor email access (enabled by default), knowledge of the donor email address, and an account already linked to the targeted donor record are required. NOTE: This vulnerability can be chained with CVE-2026-82676 to satisfy the administrator donor pre-requisite for a targeted administrator user attack. Exploitable remotely over the network.
solution: Enforce authentication on every affected endpoint/server-side; do not rely on client checks. Update to the patched version.

problem: Logto is the modern, open-source auth infrastructure for SaaS and AI apps. Prior to 1.46.0, social account linking can use an unverified email returned by the standard OAuth 2.0 or Azure AD connector to select an existing local account. When findSocialRelatedUser matches a victim's email and a request to POST /api/experience/identification enables linkSocialIdentity, an attacker who controls that unverified provider email can link an attacker-controlled social identity to the victim account and sign in as the victim. The issue applies when the provider does not verify email ownership or allows the value to be set freely; Google, GitHub, and default OIDC connector behavior is not affected because those paths expose only verified email. Version 1.46.0 adds an opt-in email synchronization control to the standard OAuth 2.0 connector, while the Azure AD connector has offered an equivalent opt-in control since version 1.43.0. These controls preserve existing behavior by default, so administrators must enable them on affected connectors. A configurable mitigation is available in version 1.46.0. Exploitable remotely over the network.
solution: Enforce authentication on every affected endpoint/server-side; do not rely on client checks. Update to the patched version.

problem: The WPvivid — Backup, Migration & Staging plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Arbitrary File Deletion in version up to, and including, 0.9.134. problem: @fastify/http-proxy is a Fastify plugin that proxies HTTP and WebSocket traffic to an upstream server. In versions from 9.0.0 up to but not including 11.6.10, when the plugin is registered with websocket support enabled, it takes every upgraded socket and dispatches the request through the Fastify router before the WebSocket library takes ownership of the socket. Node.js removes its own error listener from the socket before emitting the upgrade event, and the plugin does not attach one of its own during routing, so a socket error such as a client connection reset that arrives before the WebSocket library takes over is unhandled and terminates the Node.js process. The error window is open whenever anything asynchronous runs between dispatch and the route handler, such as an async hook on the proxied route or any unrelated async route in the application. A single unauthenticated upgrade request followed by a connection reset is enough to crash the server, and it can be repeated to keep the process down. The issue is fixed in @fastify/http-proxy 11.6.10, and users should upgrade to 11.6.10 or later. Exploitable remotely over the network.
solution: Apply the vendor patch at the earliest maintenance window and confirm the asset is not internet-exposed.

problem: @fastify/http-proxy is a Fastify plugin that proxies HTTP and WebSocket traffic to an upstream server. Building the upstream target then throws, the error is only logged, and the accepted client socket is left open with no error listener, so the next frame the client sends becomes an unhandled error and terminates the Node.js process. A request target that is not a valid URL reference reaching a parameterized prefix triggers the same path. A single unauthenticated upgrade request followed by one frame is enough to crash the server, and it can be repeated to keep the process down. problem: @fastify/http-proxy is a Fastify plugin that proxies HTTP and WebSocket traffic to an upstream server. The shared upgrade listener sees the socket is already claimed and returns early without taking the upgrade, but it does not attach an error listener to the raw socket, and Node.js has already removed its own error listener before emitting the upgrade event. A later socket error on that connection, such as a client connection reset, is therefore unhandled and terminates the Node.js process. A single unauthenticated connection that pipelines an upgrade behind a normal request and then resets is enough to crash the server, and it can be repeated to keep the process down. Upgrades over TLS are not affected. The issue is fixed in @fastify/http-proxy 11.6.10, and users should upgrade to 11.6.10 or later. Exploitable remotely over the network.

problem: netty-incubator-codec-ohttp implements Oblivious HTTP (OHTTP) gateway and client functionality using Netty. Prior to 0.0.23.Final, BinaryHttpParser.readFieldLine in codec-bhttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/bhttp/BinaryHttpParser.java treats a complete field line that ends exactly at a known field-section boundary as incomplete and returns without consuming bytes. BinaryHttpParser.readFieldSection then leaves fieldSectionLength unchanged and repeats the loop because its forward-progress checks are Java assertions, which are normally disabled in production. A remote peer that sends a known-length Binary HTTP header or trailer section ending at that boundary can make the parser spin indefinitely and pin the Netty event-loop or worker thread responsible for the channel. problem: FlowIntel contains a resource exhaustion vulnerability in its file-to-note conversion feature. problem: @fastify/http-proxy is a Fastify plugin that proxies HTTP and WebSocket traffic to an upstream server. problem: When extra data is allowed, providing both the alias and the name of an aliased TypedDict or dataclass field makes the unvalidated value (provided under the name) overwrite the validated one (provided under the alias), resulting in validated data not matching the declared type. Extra items are stored in the same dictionary as the fields (the returned dictionary for TypedDict, the instance __dict__ for dataclasses). As only the alias is marked as used, the field name is treated as an extra item, and its unvalidated value overrides the validated one. The TypedDict validator (pydantic-core/src/validators/typed_dict.rs) and the dataclass validator (pydantic-core/src/validators/dataclass.rs) share this logic. The issue was fixed in commit 34491f5328f168f14e3769cd5f0f83c0af0f4778. Impact: validation bypass, as data returned by validation doesn't match the declared type. Affected are applications validating untrusted data into TypedDict or dataclass types with aliased fields and extra data allowed (with extra='allow', or with the extra_items argument for TypedDict), using Pydantic V2 (up to and including 2.14.1). Pydantic models (BaseModel) are not affected, as extra data is stored separately from fields. Exploitable remotely over the network.
solution: Allowlist and validate all input server-side before use. Update to the patched version.

problem: Flowintel contains a privilege escalation vulnerability in its Matrix relay (bot) integration. When the relay forwarded API requests on behalf of a represented user, the authorization and permission checks evaluated the relay bot's elevated role while the request handlers acted as the lower-privileged represented user. This mismatch allowed users with restricted roles (e.g., Read Only) to perform write operations, directory lookups, calendar modifications, assignment changes, template creation, and import actions they were not authorized to perform. Additionally, relay authority was determined by matching editable user profile fields (name and email) rather than a protected, non-spoofable identifier. An ordinary user who modified their profile to match the expected bot name could be recognized as the trusted relay, enabling impersonation of the bot and potential access to its elevated privileges. Preconditions: - A valid Flowintel user account with a restricted role (e.g., Read Only) - Access to the Matrix relay integration or the ability to send API requests with the relay's API key and a MATRIX-ID header - For the impersonation vector: ability to edit one's own profile name fields Security impact: - Unauthorized write operations by users with read-only or otherwise restricted permissions - Potential impersonation of the trusted relay bot by ordinary users - Bypass of organization-level access controls and role-based restrictions - Unauthorized modification of cases, tasks,… Exploitable remotely over the network.
solution: Enforce authentication on every affected endpoint/server-side; do not rely on client checks. Update to the patched version.

problem: FlowIntel contained a Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) vulnerability affecting fourteen web routes that performed destructive or state-changing operations. The affected routes accepted HTTP GET requests in addition to (or instead of) POST, which bypassed the Flask-WTF CSRF token validation that is only enforced on non-GET requests. The vulnerable operations included: - Case deletion and case merging - Organisation removal from a case - Task deletion (case and template) - Case template and note template deletion - Connector, connector instance, and icon deletion - Custom tag deletion and status change - Taxonomy and galaxy status changes An attacker who could induce an authenticated user to follow a crafted link or load a page containing a cross-site navigation (e.g., an image tag or redirect) could trigger any of these destructive actions using the victim's session cookie, without the victim's explicit consent or awareness. No special privileges beyond a valid authenticated session with the appropriate role (editor or admin) were required on the victim's account. Security impact: unauthorized deletion or modification of cases, tasks, templates, connectors, icons, custom tags, taxonomies, and galaxies belonging to the victim or the organisation, resulting in loss of data integrity. Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0. Exploitable remotely over the network.
solution: Add anti-CSRF tokens to state-changing requests and check Origin/Referer. Update to the patched version.

problem: Incorrect Authorization vulnerability in phoenixframework phoenix_live_view allows an authenticated user to mount a router-mounted LiveView without the on_mount hooks of its live_session via a phx_join message that carries neither a "url" nor a "redirect" key. The catch-all clause of the private Phoenix.LiveView.Channel.authorize_session/3 in lib/phoenix_live_view/channel.ex accepts a join without a URL for any session, including a root LiveView mounted at the router. The channel then mounts the LiveView with no route, and only a route adds the live_session hooks to the mount lifecycle. Checks that those hooks perform on the connected mount do not run, and event checks that they attach through attach_hook/4 are never attached. The attacker needs a valid session token for the LiveView, which only the HTTP render issues, after the hooks pass there. on_mount hooks declared in the LiveView module still run. This issue affects phoenix_live_view: from 0.16.0 before 1.0.20, from 1.1.0-rc.0 before 1.1.34, and from 1.2.0-rc.0 before 1.2.14. Exploitable remotely over the network.

problem: FlowIntel's chatbot component used a single shared MCP (Model Context Protocol) session and process-wide environment variable to pass per-user API credentials to a child process. Because the session and the ambient FLOWINTEL_API_KEY environment variable were shared across all concurrent requests, a user's authenticated identity could be applied to another user's tool invocation, or a stale/ambient credential could be inherited by a new request. Preconditions: - An authenticated user with access to the chatbot interface. - Concurrent or overlapping chatbot tool invocations from different users, or a request made after another user's credentials were written to the process environment. Impact: - A lower-privilege user could read data belonging to a higher-privilege user (e.g., private investigation cases). - A user whose session was invalidated (deleted, password changed, key revoked) could still operate under a previously cached ambient credential. - The parent process environment was mutated with user-specific secrets, creating a persistent credential leak surface. Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0. Exploitable remotely over the network.
solution: Strip debug/verbose data and stack traces from responses; restrict sensitive endpoints. Update to the patched version.

problem: When message history is serialized and loaded again, a tool result that contains a JSON object in the serialized shape of one of Pydantic AI's file types is rebuilt as that file. History that a client submits through the Vercel AI or AG-UI adapter in the default mode is not affected. The issue is fixed in pydantic-ai and pydantic-ai-slim 1.107.10 and 2.66.0. problem: flowintel contains an authorization bypass in the file-to-note conversion feature for case tasks. problem: FlowIntel contains an authorization bypass in its case serialization logic that allows an authenticated user to view metadata of private cases they do not have access to. problem: FlowIntel, a threat intelligence case management platform, contains an information disclosure vulnerability in its case serialization logic. Preconditions: - An authenticated user account with at least read access to the affected case - The case must have connector instances attached that belong to other users or organizations Impact: - Disclosure of personal connector endpoints and credentials of other users - Disclosure of organization-scoped connector metadata across organizational boundaries - Enumeration of connector infrastructure (URLs, UUIDs, descriptions) not intended for the viewer Affected versions: < 4.1.0. problem: FlowIntel contains an authorization bypass in its task management workflow. When a user reopens a completed task (by toggling its completion state or changing its status to a non-finished value) or creates a new task within a completed privileged case, the parent case is automatically revived (un-completed, status reset to Created, finish date cleared). This could disrupt case lifecycle management, clear completion metadata, and potentially expose the case to further unauthorized modifications. problem: flowintel contains an authorization flaw in its recurring reminder notification subsystem. When a user is subscribed to recurring notifications for a case, the system does not re-verify the recipient's current access rights to that case before generating or displaying the notification. As a result, a user who previously had access to a private case and later had that access revoked can still: - Receive recurring reminder notifications containing case-related content. - View stored reminder notifications in their notification list, including notification counts, even though they no longer have permission to view the underlying case. The vulnerability affects both the notification creation path (recurring reminder generation) and the notification display path (listing and counting stored reminders). The issue arises because the authorization check performed at subscription time is not re-applied at delivery or retrieval time. Security impact is limited to information disclosure: an unauthorized user may observe case titles, reminder messages, and associated metadata that they no longer have permission to access. No integrity or availability impact is indicated by the patch. Affected versions: flowintel prior to 4.1.0. Exploitable remotely over the network.
solution: Add server-side authorization checks for every object and action. Update to the patched version.

problem: FlowIntel's alerting module contained an authorization bypass in the alert access control logic. When an alert was linked to a private case, the system relied solely on connector ownership (user or organization) to determine access, without verifying that the requesting user still held valid membership in the associated private case. This meant that a user who was a connector owner of an alert could continue to read alert details, review history, raw payloads, and action comments, and could perform review-status updates or case-creation actions, even after their access to the linked private case had been revoked or they were never a member of that case. Additionally, a time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) gap existed: after a review-status update or a competing case-creation claim was committed, the response could disclose private case identifiers or review history to a user whose access had been concurrently removed by another session linking the alert to a private case. Impact: - Unauthorized disclosure of private case data (review comments, raw payloads, action history) through alert endpoints. - Unauthorized modification of alert review status and creation of cases from alerts the user should no longer access. - Leakage of a competing case identifier to an unauthorized user during concurrent case-creation races. Affected versions: FlowIntel prior to 4.1.0. Exploitable remotely over the network.
solution: Add server-side authorization checks for every object and action. Update to the patched version.

problem: flowintel is a case management application that enforces an approval workflow for tasks in privileged cases. An authenticated user with the ability to create tasks from templates or to instantiate cases from templates could therefore place tasks directly into an active state within privileged cases, circumventing the intended approval gate. problem: vulnerability-lookup prior to version 7.1.0 contains two security issues in its web interface. First, the /user/toggle_2fa endpoint accepted HTTP GET requests and disabled the authenticated user's two-factor authentication without requiring password confirmation. Because the state-changing operation was reachable via GET, an attacker with a basic account could embed an image element (or any other GET-triggering markup) in a comment pointing to that endpoint. When a victim with 2FA enabled viewed the comment, their browser silently issued the GET request, disabling the victim's second factor of authentication. No CSRF token was enforced on the GET path, and no password was required to confirm the action. Second, the comment detail page (/comment/<uuid>) rendered unpublished comments to any visitor who possessed the URL, bypassing the moderation workflow that was intended to keep such content hidden until approved. The API correctly restricted access, but the web view did not enforce the same authorization check. The combined effect allows an attacker to degrade a victim's account security (removal of 2FA) through a single page view and to read content that was not yet approved for public release. This product adopts a rolling release strategy to maintain continuous delivery. Therefore, version details for affected or updated releases cannot be specified. The project was informed of the problem early through an issue report but has not responded yet. Exploitable remotely over the network.
solution: Allowlist and validate all input server-side before use. Update to the patched version.
